content: The Truenat test operates similarly to the Xpert MTB/RIF test. Moderate complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2021, are designed to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and resistance to rifampicin (RIF) and isoniazid (INH). Currently, tests from four manufacturers have been reviewed and recommended for use exclusively on respiratory samples. These include: Abbott RealTime MTB and Abbott RealTime MTB RIF/INH (Abbott), FluoroType MTBDR and FluoroType MTB (Bruker/Hain Life Science), BD MAX MDR-TB (Becton Dickinson), cobas MTB and cobas MTB-RIF/INH (Roche). Simultaneous detection of MTBC and RIF resistance is applicable to the Xpert MTB/RIF, Xpert Ultra, and other moderate complexity automated NAATs. The Truenat MTB or MTB Plus test requires subsequent testing with Truenat MTB-RIF Dx for RIF resistance detection. Some moderate complexity automated NAATs, such as Abbott RealTime MTB and cobas MTB, allow for either simultaneous or manual reflex testing for RIF or INH resistance (or both). For two-step procedures, the same DNA sample isolated during the initial test is used. The TB-LAMP test detects only MTBC and requires a fresh specimen for subsequent testing with an alternative molecular test or phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) to detect RIF resistance. WHO recommends using molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostics (mWRDs), such as Xpert MTB/RIF, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, Truenat MTB, Truenat MTB Plus, Truenat MTB-RIF Dx, TB-LAMP, or moderate complexity automated NAATs, as the initial diagnostic test for individuals with signs and symptoms of tuberculosis (TB). This recommendation applies to all individuals, including those with a history of TB treatment or those lost to follow-up. TB programs are encouraged to transition from microscopy to mWRDs as the initial diagnostic test due to their higher sensitivity and ability to simultaneously detect RIF resistance (and INH resistance for moderate complexity automated NAATs). The Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra tests are specifically recommended for extrapulmonary TB and pediatric cases. These tests are suitable for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in TB meningitis, lymph node aspirates, lymph node biopsies, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, or urine for extrapulmonary TB. Blood samples may also be used for HIV-positive individuals with signs of disseminated TB. Sample-specific optimization steps may be required for paucibacillary samples to achieve optimal results. For children with pulmonary TB symptoms, Xpert MTB/RIF can be used as the initial diagnostic test with sputum, gastric aspirates, nasopharyngeal aspirates, or stool samples. Xpert Ultra is recommended for sputum and nasopharyngeal aspirates. In settings with a pretest probability of 5% or higher and a negative Xpert MTB/RIF or Ultra result, repeated testing with the same or different specimen types (for a total of two tests) may be considered. Otherwise, repeat testing is not recommended. The Truenat MTB and MTB Plus tests have limited data on their performance in people living with HIV (PLHIV) and smear-negative patients. Recommendations for their use in PLHIV are based on indirect data. In children, sufficient data support their use with sputum samples only, with no data available for other specimen types. Their performance for detecting extrapulmonary TB is unknown. The TB-LAMP test is recommended as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy in settings with low HIV and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) prevalence. However, it does not provide information on RIF resistance. Moderate complexity automated NAATs are recommended for PLHIV, but data on their performance in smear-negative samples are limited to TB detection and do not include RIF or INH resistance. Data stratified by HIV status are unavailable. Recommendations for adolescents and children are based on generalizations from adult data. False-negative or indeterminate results may occur in children with paucibacillary TB. mWRDs are not recommended for treatment monitoring due to the potential for positive results from dead bacilli. Instead, microscopy and culture should be used for monitoring, following national guidelines and WHO recommendations. For MTBC detection, mWRD results are typically reported as MTB not detected, MTBC detected, no result, error, or invalid. Semi-quantitative results (high, medium, low, or very low) are provided by some mWRDs, with Xpert Ultra including an additional trace category. All semi-quantitative categories, including trace, are considered bacteriological confirmation of TB. However, in individuals evaluated for pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, a trace result may indicate non-viable bacilli rather than active TB, particularly in those treated within the past five years. Clinical decisions should be based on all available information and clinical judgment. For RIF and INH resistance detection, mWRDs report results as resistance detected, not detected, or indeterminate. Resistance may be inferred rather than directly detected in some cases. mWRDs do not eliminate the need for conventional culture-based phenotypic DST, which remains necessary to assess resistance to other anti-TB agents and monitor the emergence of additional drug resistance. If mWRD results indicate MTBC detected, RIF resistance not detected, and INH resistance is either not detected or unknown, the patient should be started on a first-line TB drug regimen per national guidelines. Additional DST may be required in cases of high risk for INH resistance, as molecular tests may miss 6–14% of INH resistance. Phenotypic DST for RIF may also be requested if the patient is at risk for RIF-resistant TB despite initial susceptibility results. If mWRD results indicate MTBC detected, RIF resistance detected, regardless of INH results, an MDR-TB risk assessment is necessary. In high MDR-TB burden countries, all TB patients are considered at high risk for MDR-TB. Patients at high risk should be initiated on an MDR/RR-TB regimen per national guidelines.
